units.title: The next-token objective: shifts, masks and perplexity
outcomes: Derive token-weighted cross-entropy and perplexity with an explicit valid-token mask.
Explain the input-target shift and predict the failure when labels are off by one.
Explain which positions a packed or padded batch must exclude from the loss and why.
units.why: Every later number in this section, from optimizer steps to evaluation claims, reads off this loss. A shifted-by-one or unmasked loss trains the wrong objective while the curve still falls.

next.note: Feed correctly shifted and masked batches from a real data loader.
Carry perplexity into evaluation and learn when it misleads.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook 10-training-loss: shift, hand loss and valid tokens
study.locator: Sections 1 (input and label shift on [1, 3, 4, 5, 6]), 3 (hand-computed cross-entropy from logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.1, -1.0]), 10 (perplexity table) and 11 (shift in the data versus shift in the model), plus Homework 3 (mean over valid tokens only)

focus: Position i predicts token i+1 from context 1 to i. Inputs and labels are the same sequence offset by one.
The mean runs over valid tokens only. Padding and -100 label positions leave both the sum and the count.
Perplexity is exp of the mean cross-entropy, so it reads as the effective shortlist size at each step.
One forward pass yields every position's distribution at once, which is why training parallelizes but generation does not.
units.reproduce: From a 2 by 3 logit batch and its targets, derive the per-position losses, the masked mean and the perplexity by hand, then match F.cross_entropy on the flattened tensors.
traps: Averaging over all positions including padding. The denominator changes, so short and padded batches get different objectives.
Shifting twice: slicing tokens in the data loader and again inside the model. Every target then predicts two steps ahead.
Comparing perplexity across tokenizers. Different vocabularies split the same text into different token counts, so the means are over different units.

selfTest.q: Why does the Raschka code flatten logits to (B*T, V) before calling cross_entropy?
selfTest.a: The function expects a 2D (N, C) input with one target index per row. Flattening keeps one row per position while targets flatten to (N,), so each position is scored against its own shifted target.

selfTest.q: Logits are [2.0, 1.0, 0.1, -1.0] and the correct token is 0. What is the loss?
selfTest.a: About 0.45. Softmax gives the correct token probability exp(2.0) / (exp(2.0) + exp(1.0) + exp(0.1) + exp(-1.0)) = 0.64, and -log(0.64) = 0.45.

selfTest.q: Labels are not shifted, so position i supervises with token i. What breaks?
selfTest.a: The model is asked to output a token already in its context, so it learns copying. The loss still falls, but the trained objective is not next-token prediction and the perplexity is meaningless.

selfTest.q: Six positions have losses [0.2, 0.4, 1.0, 0.3, 0.8, 0.5] with labels [10, 11, -100, 3, -100, 12]. What is the training loss?
selfTest.a: 0.35. Only the four positions with real labels count: (0.2 + 0.4 + 0.3 + 0.5) / 4. Including the masked positions changes both the sum and the denominator.

units.title: Feeding the model: batches, initialization and first steps
outcomes: Build a batch sampler that draws uniform random windows with correct input-target pairing.
Apply the assignment initialization recipe per module type and explain each choice.
Run overfit-one-batch and shuffled-label controls and read the verdict from each.
units.why: Silent data bugs, from ordered batches to bad initialization, waste every GPU hour after them. Two tiny controls on CPU catch them in minutes before any real run.

next.note: Hand the batches to AdamW and count the global token batch.
Watch the first steps for exploding norms and overflow.

study.locator: Section 5.1, Data Loader (pp. 34 to 35): (batch_size, context_length) input and target pairs, targets offset by one, random start indices and memory-mapped loading with np.memmap

study.title: CS336 Assignment 1 handout: debugging controls
study.locator: Section 7.2.3, Tips and tricks for debugging model architectures (p. 40): overfit a single minibatch to near-zero loss, inspect tensor shapes in a debugger, monitor activation, weight and gradient norms

focus: Each row draws its own random start in [0, n - m), so a start never runs past the end of the token array.
Inputs and targets share the same device as the model. The handout CPU tip names cpu and mps explicitly.
Linear, embedding and norm layers get different initial scales because they play different roles in the first forward pass.
The two controls answer different questions: overfitting one batch proves the pipeline works, failing on shuffled labels proves learning reads the real signal.
units.reproduce: Write get_batch from scratch: memory-mapped load, uniform random starts, and (B, m) input and target tensors with targets offset by one.
traps: Sampling a start index up to n instead of n - m. The window reads past the array end or wraps into unrelated tokens.
Initializing every weight to zero or one constant. Symmetric weights get identical gradients and never break symmetry.
Judging initialization from the first-step loss alone. A healthy init shows in stable norms and in the overfit control, not in one number.

selfTest.q: The token array has n = 100 entries and context length m = 7. Which start indices are valid?
selfTest.a: 0 through 92, which is 93 values. The window needs m tokens plus one target, so the last start is n - m - 1 = 92.

selfTest.q: Why must the sampled batch sit on the same device string as the model?
selfTest.a: PyTorch ops across devices raise an error, and silent host-device copies would stall the loop. The handout tip says to pass cpu or mps for both data and model on non-CUDA machines.

selfTest.q: Overfit-one-batch stalls at high loss. What does that verdict mean?
selfTest.a: The pipeline or model is broken, not the data. Check tensor shapes, the label shift, the learning rate and whether any parameter is frozen or detached.

selfTest.q: Why does the recipe give RMSNorm ones but small truncated weights to linear and embedding layers?
selfTest.a: Norms start as identity so they pass activations through, while small weights keep first-step activations and gradients finite. Large or constant init risks exploding or vanishing gradients before step one.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook 10-training-loss: mini Trainer and batch arithmetic
study.locator: Section 6 (mini Trainer skeleton with optimizer and scheduler step order) and Homework 2 (effective batch size from per-device batch, GPU count and accumulation steps)

focus: Weight decay sits outside the gradient in AdamW: parameters shrink by alpha times lambda directly, not through the moments.
The schedule is a pure function of t, so resuming needs t itself rather than a schedule object.
Global tokens per optimizer step equal sequences times length times accumulation times data-parallel width.
Warmup length scales with total steps, not as a fixed constant, which is why Appendix D states it as a fraction.
units.reproduce: Derive one scalar AdamW update from Algorithm 1, the learning rate at a step inside each of the three schedule phases, and the step count for a 327.68M-token budget.
traps: Adding weight decay to the gradients and calling it AdamW. That is Adam with L2, and the decay gets divided by the adaptive denominator.
Stepping the scheduler per microbatch under accumulation. The schedule then decays faster than intended because it sees more steps.
Comparing two runs by step count at different batch sizes. Fix tokens first: batch times steps times length is the common currency.

selfTest.q: How does AdamW apply weight decay differently from Adam with L2 regularization?
selfTest.a: AdamW subtracts alpha times lambda times theta from the parameters directly. With L2 in Adam, the decay enters the gradient and is rescaled by the adaptive denominator, so large-gradient parameters get less decay.

selfTest.q: Per-device batch 2, 4 GPUs, 8 accumulation steps. What is the effective batch size?
selfTest.a: 64 samples. 2 times 4 times 8 accumulation groups form one optimizer step, matching the notebook Homework 2 assert.

selfTest.q: Batch size 1024, context 256, budget 327.68M tokens. How many optimizer steps?
selfTest.a: 1250. Each step consumes 1024 times 256 = 262144 tokens, and 327680000 / 262144 = 1250.

selfTest.q: Training resumes at step t. What schedule state must the checkpoint hold?
selfTest.a: Only t. The schedule is a closed-form function of t, so restoring the exact step restores the exact rate. The optimizer moments are separate state and must be restored alongside.

units.title: Keeping training numerically healthy
outcomes: Explain the clipping rule, where it sits in the step order, and how it changes with a gradient scaler.
Explain autocast dtype choice and how GradScaler protects small gradients from underflow.
Log gradient norms, loss scale and skipped steps, and read overflow signals from the log.
units.why: One bad batch can end a run, and mixed precision makes bad batches likelier. Clipping, scaling and logging turn a crash into a diagnosed event with a known remedy.

next.note: Add the scaler state to the checkpoint so protection survives a restart.
Treat seed and run variability as uncertainty instead of noise to ignore.

study.title: CS336 Assignment 1 handout: gradient clipping
study.locator: Section 4.5, Gradient clipping (p. 34): the global norm rule with max M and eps 1e-6, applied in place after the backward pass

study.title: PyTorch AMP recipe: autocast, GradScaler and clipping order
study.locator: Sections Adding torch.autocast (forward under autocast, never backward), Adding GradScaler (scale, backward, conditional step, update) and Inspecting/modifying gradients (unscale_ before clipping), plus Troubleshooting for inf and NaN loss

study.title: LLMs from Scratch Appendix D: worked clipping example
study.locator: Section D.3 (L2 norm worked example on the gradient matrix G, before-and-after clipping comparison) and Section D.4 (clipping inside the modified training function)

focus: Clipping rescales the whole gradient vector when its global norm passes M. Direction is preserved; only the step length is capped.
Under a scaler, gradients are scaled by s, so unscale_ must run before the norm check or the threshold tests the wrong numbers.
Autocast keeps compute-heavy ops in float16 but reductions and the loss in float32, because they need the dynamic range.
A skipped optimizer step is protection working, not a bug. The log should show the skip, the shrunken scale and the recovery.
units.reproduce: Write the clip-then-step order for a plain loop and an AMP loop, including unscale_, the skip-on-inf rule and the per-step values to log.
traps: Clipping the scaled gradients. The norm test then uses a threshold meant for unscaled values and either never fires or always fires.
Running backward under autocast. Backward ops must run in the dtype chosen for the forward ops, outside the context.
Retrying a diverged run with the same seed and settings. The overflow recurs; lower the scale policy, the clip threshold or the learning rate first.

selfTest.q: The global gradient norm is 5 and M is 1. What does clipping do?
selfTest.a: It multiplies every gradient by about 1/5, the factor M / (norm + eps). The resulting norm sits just under 1 and the update direction is unchanged.

selfTest.q: Why must scaler.unscale_ run before gradient clipping?
selfTest.a: Backward under a scaler leaves gradients multiplied by the scale s. Clipping tests the norm against M, so on scaled values the comparison is wrong by a factor of s and corrupts the step.

selfTest.q: The scaler finds inf gradients and skips optimizer.step. What must still run, and what happens to the batch?
selfTest.a: scaler.update() still runs so the scale shrinks for the next step. The batch contributes no update; its gradients are discarded.

selfTest.q: Under autocast, linear layers run in float16 but the loss stays in float32. Why?
selfTest.a: Linears are compute-heavy and safe in half precision, while the loss is a reduction that needs float32 dynamic range. The recipe asserts output is float16 and loss is float32.

units.title: Checkpoints that really resume
outcomes: Save and load complete training state: model, optimizer, schedule step, scaler, RNG and data order.
Bind tokenizer, data and configuration identity to each checkpoint so mismatches fail loudly.
Prove interrupted training matches uninterrupted training to a stated equivalence level.
units.why: A weights-only checkpoint restarts training but not the run: learning rate, moments and data order all jump. Equivalence tests turn resume from a hope into a measured fact.

next.note: Generate from resumed weights with owned sampling policies.
Extend determinism from training into generation.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook 09-model-config: repository and config identity
study.locator: Repository File Map (config, tokenizer_config and generation_config roles) and the tokenizer_config section (special tokens, max length, truncation and padding sides)

focus: The iteration number restores the schedule exactly, the optimizer state restores the moments, and the scaler state restores the loss scale.
RNG seeds and data-loader order are training state. A fresh shuffle on resume silently starts a different run.
Equivalence needs a stated level: exact loss match for a few steps on fixed hardware, then tolerance bands beyond that.
Tokenizer and config versions pin the meaning of every saved tensor. A changed vocabulary or width redefines all IDs and shapes.
units.reproduce: Write save and load for model, optimizer, iteration, scaler and RNG seeds, then an interrupted-versus-uninterrupted equivalence test over fixed steps.
traps: Saving weights only. The resumed run restarts the schedule and moments, so loss jumps even though the model is identical.
Recreating the DataLoader without its generator state. Batches arrive in a new order and the run diverges from the uninterrupted reference.
Loading weights into an edited config. Shapes may still match while token IDs or widths mean something new, and nothing raises an error.

selfTest.q: The checkpoint holds model, optimizer and iteration. Why is the iteration number needed?
selfTest.a: It restores the schedule position. Without it the learning rate restarts at the wrong phase, for example back at the warmup peak, and the run diverges from the original.

selfTest.q: What does the CS336 test_checkpointing test actually compare?
selfTest.a: That the loaded iteration equals the saved one, that model state dicts match key by key, and that optimizer state dicts match including param groups and moment tensors.

selfTest.q: Resumed loss diverges from the uninterrupted run within a few steps. Name two suspects.
selfTest.a: Unrestored RNG or DataLoader order, which feeds different batches, and missing scaler or optimizer moment state, which changes the update itself.

selfTest.q: Why pin tokenizer_config and config versions alongside the checkpoint?
selfTest.a: Token IDs and tensor shapes are config-relative. A changed vocabulary or width silently redefines what every saved number means, so the binding must fail loudly on mismatch.
